ut_farside.blurb: A quiet bouldering area in Little Cottonwood Canyon, tucked away from the busier roadside venues. The problems are spread over a handful of boulders and run from V0 up to V10, with the heaviest concentration between V3 and V7, so there is something for most levels. Its distance from the crowds makes it a good fallback on days when the canyon's other boulder fields are packed. Bring pads suited to a walk-in, since it takes a bit of effort to reach.
ut_farside.approach: From the lot, join the paved bike path, cross the river, then pick up the climbers' trail that branches off to the right and follow it uphill for roughly ten minutes.

ut_fucoidal_quartzite.blurb: A popular roadside crag in Logan Canyon, built on textured, solid quartzite with black and white rippled patterns that make distinctive holds. It is mostly bolted sport climbing with a smaller share of trad and a few longer routes, and the bulk of the climbs fall between 5.10 and 5.12. The walls sit in the trees a short scramble above the pavement and tend to feel warm, which helps in a canyon that is otherwise cool. Expect company on good days, and note that Logan Canyon runs cold enough that winter rock climbing is rarely pleasant.

ut_ice_cream_parlor.blurb: A busy crag in Kane Springs Canyon west of Moab, on Wingate sandstone and nearby Navajo rock. Climbs are mostly single pitch and split between trad cracks and bolted slabs, with the bulk of them between 5.9 and 5.11, plus a few multipitch lines on the lower left. The middle slabs offer plenty of moderates, while the steeper rock to the right holds some of the best and quietest climbing. The cliff faces west, so it is pleasant in the morning on hot days and cools off by afternoon. Weekdays are calmer, since groups and dusty off-road traffic fill the canyon on weekends. Carry plenty of water in summer.

ut_public_service_wall.blurb: A long sandstone wall in Indian Creek, tucked behind the Fin Wall. The climbing is all trad on Wingate sandstone cracks, concentrated between 5.10 and 5.12, with only a few easier options. It was a busy destination decades ago and later faded from attention, so it still holds plenty of overlooked lines and tends to be less crowded than the headline walls. Reach it by hiking in from the Fin Wall area and curling around the buttress. Facilities in the Creek are minimal, so pack out your waste, and treat the sandstone gently since wet rock is fragile.

ut_critic_s_choice.blurb: A smaller Indian Creek cliff with a mix of a few hard crack testpieces and some gentler climbing, nearly all of it trad on Wingate sandstone. Grades run from 5.9 to 5.13, with most between 5.10 and 5.11. The wall picks up morning sun and goes into shade in the afternoon through summer. The rock has some loose and freshly fallen pieces, so move carefully near the base and test holds. Two well-marked trails climb from the parking area at the end of a rough high-clearance track, one up a wash to the left side and the other toward the talus on the right.

ut_black_and_tan_2.blurb: One of three limestone sport crags off Woodbury Road, south of the Utah hills near St. George. The rock is rough, sharp and striped in black and tan, with a character that is thin and technical. Nearly everything is bolted, and the difficulty skews hard: most routes sit between 5.10 and 5.13, with a handful of easier lines in the 5.6 to 5.8 range. It is a short stroll from neighboring Kelly's Rock, and the access road is graded enough for an ordinary car. This is a remote spot with no facilities, so bring water and supplies.

ut_sabbatical_wall.blurb: A tall, west-facing wall in Indian Creek, shaded until late morning or into the afternoon. The climbing is almost entirely trad on sandstone cracks, with most routes between 5.10 and 5.12 and very little that is truly easy. Some lines are long enough to call for a 70 meter rope or two ropes. The approach follows a defined but loose path along a ridge on the right side of the wall, and takes a fair walk. Some anchors are worn, so carry spare webbing or quick links. Avoid climbing on damp sandstone.
ut_sabbatical_wall.approach: A well-worn but loose trail climbs a hogback along the right edge of the wall, reaching the base near a cluster of short moderate cracks.

ut_crescent_crack_buttress.blurb: A popular granite buttress in Little Cottonwood Canyon, named for a long, curving crack that defines its face. Four sectors hold mostly trad routes with a smaller number of bolted lines, with most grades between 5.8 and 5.11. The walk-in is short and easy to follow, which makes it a good place for a quick day on crack climbing. Most routes can be descended by rappelling with a single rope, and the main crack is descended down a gully to the east.
ut_crescent_crack_buttress.parking_note: Use the park-and-ride lot at the mouth of the canyon. The climbers' trail begins at the lot's far corner, close to the restroom.
ut_crescent_crack_buttress.approach: Take the trail east until you are right below the buttress, then bear left at the fork. A short walk brings you to the base of the routes.
